messages.subject: D4 MCDS analysis
parts:
Hi Dan,

I'm cc'ing your message and my reply to the distance-sampling list, as it's
the kind of question I've been asked before. Others: don't bother reading if
you're not interested in MCDS (i.e., multiple covariates) analyses.

On Fri, 14 Mar 2003 14:29:33 +0100, Daniel Pike wrote:

> >Hi Len

> >I downloaded the new D4 and was running some covariate analyses. I noticed
> >something strange. For most of the covariates, the AIC is exactly the same.
> >For all of them, the estimated esw is exactly the same. I have a feeling
> >something worse than chance must be involved here...

> >I've attached the file, and look in the set called COV. The one at the top
> >is the simple model, the rest are covariate models. Just doesn't seem
> >possible to me, that the covariates would all result in the same AIC and
ESW.

> >Thanks,

> >Daniel.

For other people's benifit: the analyses you sent use the hazard rate key
function with no covariates. You started with a CDS analysis (ie no
covariates), and that had AIC 1376.68. Then you tried different covariates:
BSS, CLOUD, SIGHT and GLARE (all non-factor), all of which had AIC to two
decimal places of 1379.51, and OBS (factor, with 3 levels) which had AIC of
1381.51.

When you look at the results of the covariate analyses you can see that the
results are actually slightly different, just at more than two decimal
places. In each case, the parameter(s) corresponding to the covariate values
are estimated to be almost zero -- in other words the covariate is having
almost no affect on the analysis. For example, the BSS covariate, from the
Detection Fct/Global/Model Fitting page:

Model
Hazard Rate key, k(y) = 1 - Exp(-(y/s)**-A(2))

s = A(1) * Exp(fcn(A(3))) !

Parameter A(1) is the intercept of the scale parameter s.
Parameter A(2) is the power parameter.
Parameter A(3) is the coefficient of covariate BSS.
A( 1) bounds = ( 14.000 , 0.10000E+07 )
A( 2) bounds = ( 1.0000 , 35000. )

Iter LN(likelihood) Parameter Values
-------------------------------------------------------------------
0 -686.753 336.574 3.00000 0.000000
1 -686.753 336.574 3.00000 -0.859340E-14
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Results:
Convergence was achieved with 2 function evaluations.
Final Ln(likelihood) value = -686.75342
Akaike information criterion = 1379.5068

Parameter A(3) corresponds to the BSS covariate, and its value is estimated
to be -0.85x10-14 -- pretty small! On the next page of results, you get a
standard error for this parameter: 0.1204.

Same for all the other covariates, which is explains why ESW, etc for all the
covariate analyses are almost exactly the same.

One thing I did notice, however, is that the maximum likelihood found by the
MCDS analysis is "wrong". Remember that AIC is -2*Lnl + 2*k where k is the
number of parameters. In the CDS analysis, k is 2 (2 hazard rate
parameters), and in the non-factor MCDS analyses, k is 3 (2 hazard rate
parameters + the covaraite. When the covariate is having almost no effect,
we expect the log likelihood for both CDS and MCDS analyses to be almost
exactly the same -- so the AIC for the MCDS analysis should be almost exactly
2 higher than the CDS analysis. But in this case it wasn't: 1376.68 for CDS
and 1379.51 for MCDS. It's more than two higher.

This implies that the MCDS analysis isn't finding the maximum likelihood
solution. CDS and MCDS analysis engines use different algorithms so it is
possible for this to happen. If you re-run the CDS analysis with the option
"Model Definition | Misc | Report results for each iteration of the fitting
routine" ticked, you can see that it doesn't head straight for the maximum
likelihood solution but that -Lnl actually gets higher in one iteration. You
can also see that the final parameter estimates for the two hazard rate
parameters are different from the MCDS analyses (they are 301.528 and 2.66381
in the CDS analysis, which gives -Lnl -686.389 -- lower than the -686.753
found by the MCDS routine with parameters 336.574 and 3.000 and the very
small BSS parameter).

A solution is to start the MCDS routine off with the maximum likelihood
estimates from the CDS analysis, and 0.000 for the 3rd parameter (the
covariate parameter). You set starting values in Model Definition |
Detection Function | Adjustment terms | Manually set starting values. The
number of parameters in this case is 3, and I entered the values 301.518,
2.66381, and 0.0. Now I get

Iter LN(likelihood) Parameter Values
-------------------------------------------------------------------
0 -686.389 301.528 2.66381 0.000000
1 -686.386 301.533 2.69137 -0.843569E-03
2 -686.386 301.533 2.69137 -0.843569E-03
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Results:
Convergence was achieved with 3 function evaluations.
Final Ln(likelihood) value = -686.38578
Akaike information criterion = 1378.7716

so the difference in AIC is 1.994 -- more reasonable. As you can see -- the
effect of the covariate is still very small.

Bottom line is that in this dataset the covariates don't seem to affect the
detection function.

The trick of using CDS results as starting values for MCDS analyses is a
generally useful one -- indeed I should think about implementing it as the
default in Distance one of these days (will make computations take longer
though). The problem of not finding the maximim likelihood solution is worse
for hazard rate keys than half-normal (actually, I haven't seen an example
with half normal yet), and worse when you have several adjustment terms.

Cheers,

- Len
